fixes.explanation: David appointed stonecutters from the foreigners in the land of Israel to prepare finished stones for building the house of God. So the stones got shaped before anyone started stacking them. That's the kind of work nobody claps for. I can respect a man who gets the dough ready before the oven is even hot.

That's right, friend. The text says David provided a large quantity of iron, together with more bronze than could be weighed. That's no little bit. My kitchen scale would take one look at that pile and ask for a transfer.

Yes, friend. The text says the Sidonians and Tyrians brought David more cedar logs than could be counted. That's a pile past counting. I lose count on a long day of cookie batches, and mine only go up to about forty.

You got it, friend. David says the house to be built for the LORD must be "…exceedingly magnificent—famous and glorious throughout all lands." Then he adds, "Therefore I must make preparations for it."

That's it, friend. God said, "…I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign." That's a promise worth hearing. David had waged great wars (1 Chronicles 22:8), so I bet peace and quiet sounded GOOD.

A bigger army would make sense in a kingdom that has seen war. But God promised something different. He said He would give the son rest from all his enemies on every side and grant Israel "…peace and quiet…" That's the promise God gave about the reign.

Right, friend. David tells Solomon, "Above all, may the LORD give you insight and understanding when He puts you in command over Israel…" Solomon, David's son, has a big job coming. David puts insight and understanding above all.

With all that gold and silver lying around, wealth is an easy guess. But David doesn't wish it for Solomon. His wish is that the LORD would give Solomon insight and understanding when He puts him in command over Israel (1 Chronicles 22:12). The treasure was already gathered, and David's "above all" goes to understanding.

Victory in battle fits a king, but David doesn't wish for it here. His wish is that the LORD would give Solomon insight and understanding. The LORD had already said the son would be a man of rest (1 Chronicles 22:9). And David's "above all" goes to understanding.

David does order the leaders of Israel to help Solomon, so I see the guess. But that isn't what he says to Solomon here. He tells him, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged." That order to the leaders comes later (1 Chronicles 22:17), and Solomon is still the one being told to be strong.
You've got it, friend. David says, "…I have taken great pains to provide for the house of the LORD…" That pile of gold, silver, bronze and iron wasn't gathered easily.

That's right, friend. David says the craftsmen in gold and silver, bronze and iron are "beyond number." He also tells Solomon, "You also have many workers…" (1 Chronicles 22:15). Solomon, David's son, isn't short on skilled hands.

David did say it, friend. He tells the leaders of Israel that the LORD "…has given the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land has been subdued before the LORD and His people." He says the LORD has also granted them rest on every side.

The bronze serpent is in the Bible (Numbers 21:9), but David doesn't mention it here. He wants the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy articles of God brought into the temple. Those are the things he names (1 Chronicles 22:19). The serpent isn't on his list.
